rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Double the gradient duration while holding the window and temperature fixed to distinguish slope-responsive overlaps from pairs that need a selectivity change. The first run's early elution suggests this diagnostic run should still finish near 10 minutes.

Keep the successful shallower gradient and raise temperature to probe selectivity at the remaining close pair. Higher temperature should also create time margin below 10 minutes for further refinement.

Test the upper temperature limit with the gradient unchanged to see whether the remaining overlap separates further. The 55 C run leaves ample time margin, and the late close pair may also benefit from this selectivity shift.

Slightly flatten the gradient at the best temperature to improve the late critical pair while retaining the sub-10-minute finish. This also tests whether the early pair at R 1.61 has enough selectivity margin.

The shallower gradient worsened the late critical pair, so test a steeper gradient instead. An 18-minute gradient should improve that pair and shorten elution, while checking whether the early close pairs remain sufficiently resolved.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward while preserving injection 6's gradient slope to test a small selectivity adjustment at the pair with R 1.46. The first peak is well retained, so this trimmed window should also shorten elution without sacrificing the late-pair separation.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 to lift both early critical resolutions while retaining its improved late-pair separation. The narrower endpoint window allows an intermediate slope on the instrument grid, with ample organic strength to elute all peaks.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to push the early critical pairs above R 1.5. The late critical pair has some margin, and the last peak should still elute within the gradient and well before 10 minutes.

Injection 9 reached the maximum CRF; now test a shorter fully resolved separation by raising the starting organic fraction and narrowing the window. The shallower slope may compensate for the early-pair resolution loss seen when raising phi0 previously.

Flatten the gradient modestly at phi0 0.15 to improve the early pair that limited injection 10, while checking the late pair's remaining margin. Retain injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark if this shorter-elution branch cannot achieve full resolution.

Injection 9 already attains the maximum score, while the higher-starting-organic branch shows conflicting resolution requirements. Probe low-temperature selectivity with a faster gradient to look for an alternative fully resolved separation with shorter elution.

Raise temperature by one step while preserving injection 12's slope to test whether its single severe overlap can be removed by selectivity. This should also shorten retention, though the late pair at R 1.55 needs monitoring.

Test a steeper gradient on the low-temperature branch to determine whether slope-driven reordering can separate its central overlap. This explores a faster alternative while retaining injection 9 as the established maximum-score method.

Combine the steeper low-temperature gradient with the temperature increase that improved central selectivity in injection 13. This may resolve both limiting pairs from injection 14 while shortening its 7.30-minute last-peak time.

Test a shifted, narrower organic window to change central selectivity on the low-temperature branch while reducing retention time. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this run seeks a faster fully resolved alternative rather than a higher possible CRF.

Flatten the shifted-window gradient to spread the central overlap, using the substantial resolution margins of its neighboring pairs. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, allowing this branch to challenge the established maximum-score method.

Test a temperature-driven selectivity change at the promising shifted-window gradient, rather than further flattening a slope that trades resolution between two central pairs. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark while this run probes an alternative elution order.

Raise temperature one step to move the newly limiting central pair away from its apparent crossover, keeping the gradient fixed to isolate selectivity. This branch elutes faster than injection 9, which remains the established maximum-score method.

Test whether a shallower gradient lifts the remaining central pair above R 1.5 at 45 C. The 6.60-minute finish leaves time margin, but the late pair at R 1.77 must be checked for a competing loss of resolution.

Return to the near-resolved high-temperature branch and test whether lowering temperature improves its competing early and late overlaps. Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF; this probes a potentially faster alternative while preserving that benchmark.

Refine around the maximum-score method with a slightly shallower slope to increase the early-pair resolution margin. This tests the opposite edge of the fully resolved region, with the late critical pair expected to be the constraint.

Test an intermediate slope between injections 4 and 6 at the lower starting organic fraction, seeking a wider resolution margin than injection 9. The early and late critical pairs respond oppositely to slope, so this run checks their compromise directly.

Test a shorter programmed gradient with a lower endpoint near the observed elution window. The slightly shallower slope should improve the early pairs, but the late critical pair may fall below R 1.5; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Use the final injection to test whether ending the gradient near the late critical pair changes its separation during the hold, while the shallower slope improves the early pairs. This is exploratory; injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score method.
